title: 道德經 第六十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 69, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 87. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 69 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 玄用 (The Dark at Work). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
用兵有言﹕「
吾不敢為主而為客，
不敢進寸而退尺。」
是謂行無行，

sentences.l:
In the wielding of arms there is a saying:
'I do not dare play the host, but play the guest;
I do not dare advance an inch, but withdraw a foot.'
This is called marching where there is no line of march,
sentences.i: Those who wield arms have a saying: 'I dare not play the host, but play the guest; I dare not advance an inch, but give ground a foot.' This is what is meant by marching with no column to march in,
sentences.n:
主 and 客 are the technical words of the art of war, and they are the words for host and guest: the 主 is the side that opens the war and fights on its own ground, the 客 the side that only answers. The book has spent sixty chapters preferring the lower place, and here the preference has a battlefield in it — the aggressor loses.

寸 and 尺 are real measures, not a figure of speech: the 寸 is about a thumb's breadth, the 尺 ten of them. He will not take the small distance forward, and gives up ten times as much going back.

行無行 is the polyphone at its plainest. The first 行 is xíng, the verb 'to march'; the second is the same character read háng, the noun 'a rank, a column' — Wang Bi glosses it 行陳, the drawn-up array of an army. So: to march with no marching-order. Four clauses now run on the same paradox, verb + 無 + its own object: march with no ranks, bare the arm with no arm, close with no enemy, take hold with no weapon. The man who wants nothing offers nothing to fight.

客 kè and 尺 chǐ end their lines together and rhymed in Old Chinese — both were entering-tone words closing on -k, in the same rhyme group. Mandarin has worn both endings away and the chime is gone.

sentences.l:
baring the arm where there is no arm,
hauling where there is no enemy,
sentences.i: rolling the sleeve back on no arm, closing with no enemy,
sentences.n:
攘臂 is a whole scene in two characters — the sleeve shoved back off the forearm before a man lays hands on you. You met it in chapter 38, where the ritualist rolls up his sleeve and drags people into line when no one answers him. Here the arm is not there to bare.

扔 is rare and nobody is quite sure of it. The old dictionaries give 'to pull, to drag by force, to draw up against'; it is certainly not the modern Mandarin sense 'to throw away', which is a much later development. The Mawangdui silk manuscripts are reported to order these clauses differently and to write 乃 nǎi 'and then' where the received text has 扔 — which turns the fourth clause from a fourth paradox into a result: hold nothing, and then you have no enemy at all. The received reading is kept here and the variant left on the record.

sentences.t:
執無兵。
禍莫大於輕敵，
輕敵幾喪吾寶。

sentences.i: laying hold where there is no weapon. No calamity is greater than making light of the enemy — make light of the enemy, and my treasure is all but lost.
sentences.n:
禍莫大於 X is the frame you met in chapter 46 (禍莫大於不知足): 莫 is a negative with its own subject built in, 'nothing', and 於 after the bare adjective supplies the 'than' that 大 alone cannot. Of calamities, none is great beyond this one.

吾寶 is 'my treasure', with no number marked on it — Chinese marks none — and it reaches back two chapters, to the three treasures of chapter 67: 慈 tenderness, 儉 frugality, and never daring to take the lead. It is the first of the three that underrating an enemy destroys.

One honest difficulty. Wang Bi's comment on this line runs as though the text in front of him read 無敵, 'to be left with no adversary', rather than 輕敵, 'to make light of the adversary': he says that a man who is grieving, tender and yielding does not set out to be without a match, and that arriving at last at having no one to face is itself the great calamity. Our text prints 輕敵 twice, and the English follows the characters on the page, since those are not ours to alter. Wang Bi's reading is recorded here, not adopted.

sentences.t:
故抗兵相加，
哀者勝矣。

sentences.l:
Therefore when arms are raised and matched against each other,
the one that grieves prevails.
sentences.i: So when two armies are raised and set against each other, it is the side that grieves that wins.
sentences.n:
Two characters here mean less than they look. Wang Bi glosses 抗 by 舉, 'to raise', and 加 by 當, 'to be a match for' — so the line is simply two forces brought up and set opposite each other, not one attacking the other. Neither side is the aggressor in the grammar; the sentence is even-handed until its last word.

哀 is grief, and 哀者 is 'the one that grieves' — the side that is sorry to be there. Wang Bi says why it wins: 哀者必相惜, those who grieve cherish one another, and so do not chase advantage or dodge danger. This is the chapter's whole argument arriving: the guest rather than the host, the foot given rather than the inch taken, and now the army that mourns its own war.
